summary: High Frontier 4 All is Phil Eklund's uncompromisingly realistic space exploration simulation, where players design rockets from real physics-based components and navigate an actual solar-system map using delta-v costs. It's notoriously dense, rewarding careful route planning and technology investment over flashy action.
praised: unmatched scientific authenticity and educational depth
satisfying long-term tech and route planning
modular scenarios scale from beginner to expert
criticised: extremely steep learning curve and rulebook density
iconography and card text are notoriously hard to parse

interaction.kind: auctioning for patent cards and racing to claim the same mining/water sites first
interaction.detail: Players bid against each other for patent cards and can be locked out of a solar-system site if a rival claims and exploits it first, so there is real competition over a shared board of sites. But the bulk of play is single-player trajectory and rocket-building optimization on your own player area, which is why the game's reputation leans toward parallel play despite the auctions.
interaction.said: Frequently called a 'solo puzzle you happen to play with others' — reviewers emphasize the dense solitaire-style route/thrust optimization, with auctions and site claims as the main point of contact.

scoring.how_you_win: You send rockets to mine, refine, and found colonies across the solar system; the player with the most colonies (plus patents/cash as tiebreakers) when the game ends wins, or in the intro variant, outright first-to-colonize wins immediately.

theme.said: constantly described as 'the mechanics ARE the theme', 'you're literally doing orbital mechanics homework', 'the most simulation-accurate space game ever made'
theme.why: thrust cards are keyed to real propulsion technologies with actual specific-impulse and delta-v values, so plotting a burn from Earth to a real asteroid orbit only works if you understand real orbital mechanics

style.why: Players race an asymmetric-but-not-combative tech and trade economy with no direct conflict, letting a dense simulation of orbital mechanics decide outcomes.
